---
title: "Sleep Confidence Intervals Activity: Code Explainer"
---

This document walks through the key code patterns in the Sleep Confidence Intervals activity. The same patterns show up in HW9.

## Building the margin of error in one `summarize()`

```
sleep_stats <- sleep_data |>
  summarize(
    mean_hours = mean(hours),
    sd_hours = sd(hours),
    n = n(),
    se_hours = sd_hours / sqrt(n),
    margin_error = qt(0.975, df = n - 1) * se_hours
  )
```

Inside `summarize()`, each line can use the columns created above it. `se_hours` uses `sd_hours` and `n`, and `margin_error` uses `se_hours`. The result is a one-row table.

Using `n` instead of typing the number (like `sqrt(37)`) means the code still works if the data changes.

`qt(0.975, df = n - 1)` is the multiplier for a 95% confidence interval. It's a little more than 2 for small samples and gets closer to 1.96 as the sample grows. The 0.975 is there because a 95% interval leaves 5% outside it, split into 2.5% on each side.

## Adding the interval with `mutate()`

```
sleep_stats <- sleep_stats |>
  mutate(
    ci_lower = mean_hours - margin_error,
    ci_upper = mean_hours + margin_error
  )
```

`mutate()` adds columns to any data frame, including a one-row summary. `select()` then shows just the columns you want.

## Checking whether a claim is inside the interval

```
claims |>
  mutate(
    inside_interval = value >= sleep_stats$ci_lower & value <= sleep_stats$ci_upper
  )
```

`&` means "and": the value has to be at or above the lower bound *and* at or below the upper bound. The result is `TRUE` (inside, so the data supports the claim) or `FALSE` (outside, so it doesn't). `sleep_stats$ci_lower` pulls a single value out of the summary table.

## Shading the interval on a histogram

```
ggplot(sleep_data, aes(x = hours)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5, fill = "gray70", color = "white") +
  annotate("rect", xmin = sleep_stats$ci_lower, xmax = sleep_stats$ci_upper,
           ymin = 0, ymax = Inf, fill = "blue", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = sleep_stats$mean_hours, color = "red", linewidth = 1)
```

`annotate("rect", ...)` draws a shaded box. `xmin` and `xmax` are the interval bounds, `ymin = 0` and `ymax = Inf` make it run the full height of the chart, and `alpha` makes it see-through. `geom_vline()` draws a vertical line.

## Comparing sample sizes in one table

```
tibble(n = c(37, 74, 148)) |>
  mutate(
    se_hours = sleep_stats$sd_hours / sqrt(n),
    margin_error = qt(0.975, df = n - 1) * se_hours
  )
```

Start with a tibble that has one row per sample size, then calculate the same things for every row. The standard deviation stays the same; only `n` changes. Because of the square root, you need four times as many people to cut the margin of error in half.

## Common mistakes

**Using 0.95 instead of 0.975 for a 95% CI:**

```
# Wrong: this gives a 90% confidence interval
qt(0.95, df = 36)

# Right
qt(0.975, df = 36)
```

**Confusing standard deviation with standard error:**

```
# Standard deviation: how spread out INDIVIDUAL answers are
sd(sleep_data$hours)

# Standard error: how much the AVERAGE would vary from sample to sample
sd(sleep_data$hours) / sqrt(nrow(sleep_data))
```

The margin of error and confidence interval use the standard error. That's why the interval is much narrower than the spread of individual answers.
